problem: Learned navigation models such as GNM, ViNT and NoMaD need over 100 hours of multi-robot data, rely on pre-specified goal images and topological maps, and focus on global navigation rather than reaching or tracking a dynamic target. No embodiment-agnostic target-reaching or following policy exists that learns directly from robot-free human demonstrations.
motivation: Collecting robot data with teleoperation or reinforcement learning is costly, risky and tied to a specific embodiment. Handheld demonstrations with a depth camera need no robot, and depth input plus relative target positions could transfer across robots and scenes with little data.
key_idea: Train a diffusion policy on about 1 hour of handheld depth-camera demonstrations, conditioned on depth, the relative target position and an intermediate goal, to output normalized SE(2) waypoints that any robot can execute.
insight: Explicit target labels help substantially: ViDEN reaches 84% on hard tasks versus 16% without target labels. The simplified version (no task-agnostic data, no memory token, p_m=0.5, no target dropout) reaches only 72% on hard, so those training tricks add about 12 points. The diffusion policies beat BC-ConvMLP and ViNT (with its goal image replaced by relative distance) most on moderate and hard tasks. Fine-tuning on a new indoor environment recovers performance from 55% zero-shot.
method: Handheld demonstration collection: a person sweeps a ZED Mini depth camera toward a target, avoiding obstacles. YOLOv5 detects the target and gives its relative position s_t, and IMU plus visual odometry gives the SE(2) pose. No robot or teleoperation is involved.
Embodiment-agnostic action space: waypoints are expressed in the camera frame and normalized by the dataset's min/max velocity. At deployment they are rescaled by the robot's maximum velocity.

Goal conditioning: sequences of length h carry an intermediate goal g_t* sampled from a future time in the demonstration. At deployment the goal lies at min(λ, ||s_t||) on the line to the target, with λ=2.5 m. A memory token estimates the target when it is out of view.

Encoder: a four-layer CNN encodes the depth image, and separate MLPs encode the target and the goal. The tokens go into a four-layer transformer encoder that gives the latent z_t. Depth is clipped at 10 m and augmented with rotation, crop, blur, masking and varied time intervals.
Diffusion BC policy: a U-Net noise predictor conditioned on z_t denoises a 32-step trajectory over K=100 steps. Deployment uses 5 diffusion steps and executes a 16-step horizon.

Goal masking and task-agnostic data: the goal token is masked with probability p_m=0.7 to support exploration. 20% of the data has no target in view, and the target position is dropped out 50% of the time.
Deployment: a Jetson Orin runs the policy and a PD controller tracks the trajectory on a Unitree Go2 through ROS, with no map.

setting.backbone: CNN + transformer encoder + U-Net diffusion policy (trained from scratch); YOLOv5 for target detection
setting.training_data: 120 handheld demonstrations, about 60 min, collected outdoors with a ZED Mini (about 1.5 h in the intro); 20% task-agnostic. Fine-tuning on an indoor environment used up to 30 min of extra demonstrations.
setting.observation: Depth image (clipped at 10 m) plus a relative target position from RGB object detection
setting.action_space: Predicted normalized SE(2) waypoint trajectory (32 steps, 16 executed), tracked by a PD controller

numbers.eval_set_note: 25 trials (5 scenes x 5 runs) per difficulty level

results: ViDEN reaches 100% / 96% / 84% on easy / moderate / hard real-robot human-following. ViNT reaches 92% / 60% / 20% and BC-ConvMLP 60% / 48% / 12%. Zero-shot transfer to an unseen indoor scene gives 55%, and fine-tuning brings it close to the original environment's success rate.
limitations: Small, biased dataset from one outdoor environment, with only a human target tested and no standard benchmark; the paper reports 55% zero-shot in a new scene.
Weak robustness to physical perturbations (30%) and moderate in low light (73%).
Only planar SE(2) motion and a single quadruped robot; embodiment-agnosticism across robots is not shown, and the number of trials is small.
